  • Move faster and publish further. A native, accessible Table Studio and structured Word/CSV views; direct publishing to external platforms; and a document-audit family (ACB large-print guidelines, the Microsoft Accessibility Checker, WCAG 2.2 AA) brought in as authoring-time checks.
  • Speak even more freely. Dictation’s later phases — an optional global Windows dictation hotkey, idle-silence auto-stop, and spoken punctuation and commands — plus ElevenLabs live streaming Read Aloud and voice management beyond today’s export.
  • Solid everywhere you work. Verified installer behavior on Windows 10 and 11, shipping-quality macOS, native RTF editing, and a Quillin Hub with plugin signing and a marketplace so the community can publish the tools it wishes existed.
  • More ways in. Native Google Docs round-tripping, a deeper getting-started tutorial and walkthrough series, and a growing library of community Verbosity Packs, sound packs, and Quillins. Some of these are close; some are further out. All are built on the same promises, so nothing new will ever cost you the quiet, the privacy, or the control you have today.
Availability

QUILL is free. This public beta includes:

  • Windows installer — per-user, no admin required, with every speech engine (whisper.cpp, eSpeak-NG, DECtalk, Piper, Kokoro), Pandoc, and the braille pack bundled. Choose components during setup; a Full install includes everything.
  • Portable edition — the same fully-bundled studio in a folder you can carry on a drive, with an empty data/ folder so it works from the first launch. We keep refining QUILL with live screen-reader use across JAWS, NVDA, and Narrator, and installer verification on clean Windows 10 and 11 machines. That is work the community does best, which is why the feature set is in your hands now.
How to help shape QUILL

The fastest way to influence QUILL is to use this beta for real work — write with it, review with it, customize it, push it. Then tell us what works, what breaks, and what should be better:

  • Install or start QUILL.
  • Let it carry forward your compatible settings at startup.
  • Keep working with your familiar files and preferences.
  • Send feedback from Help > Report a Bug — bugs, accessibility issues, confusing workflows, and feature requests all land where the team can act on them. Optional extras, only if you want them: the offline speech engine ships in the installer (or drop it into tools\speech\whispercpp in a portable copy), then download a model from Manage Speech Models; ffmpeg (one click from Tools > Speech > Download FFmpeg…) lets you transcribe formats beyond WAV; and Faster Whisper adds a GPU engine on capable machines. None are required to launch, edit, or save.
A word on feedback — and a request

Please remember that this is a beta. Bugs will exist — that is the nature of a public beta, and finding them is exactly what this stage is for. We are trying very hard to stay on top of your feedback, and we will be more diligent in that process going forward. The improved crash reporting and the direct, in-app submission experience are built precisely to make that easier — for you to report and for us to act on it quickly.

And one request: be kind, and be constructive. Honest, frank feedback is welcome — we can handle that, and we genuinely want it. A small team reads every report, and a clear, generous one helps us fix the right thing faster.

About QUILL

QUILL — Quality, Usable, Inclusive, Lightweight, Literate — is a screen-reader-first writing studio from Community Access, built on the conviction that accessibility is not a feature you add at the end but the center you design around. It consolidates the durable value of a family of accessibility tools — including a private, on-device speech suite and the ChapterForge audiobook workflow — into one optional-by-design, private-by-default, keyboard-first environment. QUILL owns the editor, the focus, the undo, and the announcements; AI and every external integration are optional and off by default. Platform scope is Windows (primary) and macOS (supported).

QUILL is community-built and community-shaped. With QUILL, accessibility is not the finish line. Accessibility is where we begin.

Learn more at quillforall.org.

QUILL, Step by Step

QUILL, Step by Step

A listen-along manual.

How to read this book

This book is written to be listened to. Load it into ElevenReader, Voice Dream, or any app that reads to you, and let it play while you sit at your computer with QUILL open. When the book says “try it,” pause the reading, do the thing at your own speed, and press play again when you are ready. Nothing in this book is timed, and nothing breaks if you take a week between chapters.

Each chapter teaches one skill. Not one menu, not one list of shortcuts — one skill, the kind of thing your hands remember after you have done it three times. A chapter starts by telling you what the skill is for, walks you through it slowly, has you do it again a slightly different way, and ends by naming the two or three keystrokes worth keeping. If a chapter ends and you want to stop for the day, stop. The next chapter will assume only that you were awake for the ones before it.

Two promises about the writing. First, this book moves slowly on purpose. If you already know a thing, skip ahead; the chapter titles say plainly what each one covers. Second, this book will not spend your attention telling you how thoughtful QUILL is. You will form your own opinion. The book is here to teach, and everything else is a distraction.

One note on how keys are written. When you hear “Ctrl+S,” that means hold the Control key and press S, then let go of both. When a key has three parts, like Ctrl+Shift+P, hold the first two and press the last. There is exactly one unusual key in QUILL, and it gets its own chapter much later, after your hands already trust the ordinary ones.

That is the whole introduction. Let’s open the program.

Chapter 1: Meet the window

Start QUILL. It opens without ceremony — no splash screen, no sound, just a window. If this is the very first time QUILL has run on this computer, a short setup called Personalise QUILL may offer to ask a few questions about how you like to work. You can answer it or dismiss it; either is fine, and you can always run it again later from the Help menu. This book assumes nothing about how you answered.

The window has three parts, stacked top to bottom. At the top is the menu bar: File, Edit, and their relatives. In the middle, filling almost everything, is the editor — the place where text goes. At the bottom is the status bar, a single row of short facts about your document: where the cursor is, how many words there are, and a few more things we will meet properly later.

You are in the editor right now. Prove it: type your own name. There it is.

Now visit the other two parts and come back. Press the Alt key by itself. Focus moves up to the menu bar and lands on File. Press the Right arrow a few times and listen to the menus go by: Edit, View, and onward. Press Escape. You are back in the editor, and your name is still there. The menus never take anything away from you; Escape always walks you home.

The status bar works the same way. Press F6, and focus moves to the status bar; press F6 again or Shift+F6 to come back to the editor. You do not need anything from the status bar yet. Just know that it is a place you can visit, not just a line that sits there.

Try the round trip once more, all of it: Alt to the menus, Escape home. F6 to the status bar, back to the editor. Type another word to prove you are home.

That is the skill. The window has three parts; you can visit any of them and come home with Escape or F6, and nothing you wrote goes anywhere while you travel. Keep two keys from this chapter: Alt for the menus, and Escape for home.

Chapter 2: Type something and keep it

This chapter is the heart of the whole program: make a document, put words in it, and keep those words. Everything else in QUILL is decoration around this.

Press Ctrl+N. That makes a new, empty document. You may hear the window title change to something like “Untitled.” Untitled means the words exist only in QUILL’s memory so far — real enough to edit, not yet a file on your disk.

Type two or three sentences. Anything. What you had for breakfast. The weather. It genuinely does not matter, and nobody will read it.

Now keep it. Press Ctrl+S. Because this document has never been saved, QUILL asks where to put it and what to call it. This is the standard Windows save dialog, the same one every program uses. Type a name you will recognize — “practice” is a fine name — pick a folder you can find again, like Documents, and press Enter. The title changes from Untitled to your file’s name. The words are now on your disk.

Here is the habit that separates relaxed people from worried ones: press Ctrl+S again right now. Nothing dramatic happens — the file already has a name, so QUILL just saves it quietly. That quiet is the point. Ctrl+S costs you half a second, and after the first save it never asks questions. Press it whenever you pause to think. You will never wonder whether your last paragraph is safe, because it always will be.

Now close the document and get it back, because keeping a file is only useful if you can return to it. Press Ctrl+W. The document closes. If you had typed anything since your last save, QUILL would ask whether to save first — it will not let a close throw words away silently. Now press Ctrl+O, which opens the standard open dialog. Find your practice file, press Enter, and your sentences come back.

There is an even faster way back. Open the File menu with Alt, then arrow to Open Recent. QUILL keeps a list of files you have had open lately; your practice file is on it. Most days, the file you want is the one you were working on yesterday, and Open Recent is the shortest road there.

Do the loop once more from the top, without the book: new document with Ctrl+N, a sentence, save with Ctrl+S and name it something else, close with Ctrl+W, reopen from Open Recent. When that loop feels boring, you have it.

Keep three keys: Ctrl+N for new, Ctrl+S for save — pressed often and without thought — and Ctrl+O for open. You now know enough to use QUILL for real work. Everything after this makes the work more comfortable.

Chapter 3: When you are stuck, ask the program

You will forget things from this book. That is normal and expected, and QUILL assumes it. This chapter is about the two keys that answer questions, so that forgetting costs you ten seconds instead of a trip back to a manual.

The first key is F1. F1 answers the question “what is this thing I am standing on?” It works on nearly everything — a field in a dialog, a button, the editor itself. Try it now: press F1 in the editor. A small window opens and describes where you are and what applies here. Press Escape to close it. Now open any dialog — the Preferences window, on Ctrl+Comma, will do — move to any control in it with Tab, and press F1 again. It tells you what that control wants and what it affects. Escape closes the help, Escape again closes Preferences. Nothing was changed by looking.

The second key answers a bigger question: “what can QUILL do, and how do I say it?” Press Ctrl+Shift+P. This opens the Command Palette, which is a searchable list of every command in the program. Type a word — try “spell” — and the list narrows to commands about spelling. Arrow through them. Notice that as you move, each command’s keyboard shortcut is read along with its name. Press Escape without running anything.

That detail about shortcuts matters more than it seems. The palette is not just a launcher; it is how you learn the keyboard without studying. When you want something, open the palette and type a word for it. If you use that command twice, you will have heard its shortcut twice, and the third time you will press the shortcut instead. The palette teaches you out of needing it.

One more key for a specific moment of confusion: sometimes a menu item or a command is switched off, gray, unavailable — and nothing says why. When that happens, press Alt+F1, which is the command called Why Is This Unavailable. QUILL explains the reason in a sentence instead of leaving you to guess.

Practice the pair once. Press Ctrl+Shift+P, type “count”, and you will find Document Statistics — run it with Enter and hear how many words your practice file has. Then press F1 somewhere, anywhere, and close it. Those two keys are the whole skill.

Keep two keys: F1 asks “what is this?”, and Ctrl+Shift+P asks “how do I…?” Between them, you can stop memorizing and start looking things up in place.

Chapter 4: Moving through a document

So far your documents have been three sentences long, and the arrow keys were all you needed. Real documents are longer, and this chapter is about crossing them without wearing out the Down arrow.

First, the keys Windows gives every editor, in case nobody ever showed you. Left and Right move by character. Ctrl+Left and Ctrl+Right move by word, and this pair alone doubles most people’s speed. Home goes to the start of the line, End to the end of it. Ctrl+Home jumps to the very top of the document, Ctrl+End to the very bottom. Page Up and Page Down move a screenful at a time.

Open your practice file and spend one unhurried minute with just those: word by word across a sentence, Home and End a few times, Ctrl+End to the bottom, Ctrl+Home back to the top. These keys work identically in almost every program on your computer, so this minute pays rent everywhere.

Now the QUILL-specific ones. Press Ctrl+G, and a small dialog asks for a line number. Type 1 and press Enter — you are on line one. This is Go to Line, and it matters most when something else tells you a number: an error message from some tool, or a friend saying “the odd sentence is around line forty.”

Next, a kind of travel you cannot get from arrow keys at all: going back to where you just were. QUILL remembers where your cursor has been, the way a web browser remembers pages. Press Alt+Left, and the cursor returns to its previous location — for instance, the place you were before that Ctrl+G. Press Alt+Right to go forward again. Try it: Ctrl+End to the bottom, then Alt+Left. You are back where you started, not because you retraced your steps, but because QUILL kept the trail.

This back-and-forward pair changes how it feels to check something far away. Jump anywhere, look at whatever you needed, press Alt+Left, and you are home. The fear of losing your place is what makes long documents tiring, and this is the key that removes it.

Keep three things: Ctrl+Left and Ctrl+Right for words, Ctrl+Home and Ctrl+End for the ends of the document, and Alt+Left to go back to where you just were. Longer documents will stop feeling like long hallways.

Chapter 5: Selecting text

Selecting is how you tell QUILL “I mean this part.” Everything you do to text — copying it, deleting it, making it bold someday — starts by marking which text you mean. There are two ways to select in QUILL: the Windows way, and a second way that is kinder to your hands on big selections. You need both.

The Windows way first: hold Shift while you move. Every movement key from the last chapter selects when Shift is held. Shift+Right selects a character. Ctrl+Shift+Right selects a word. Shift+End selects to the end of the line. Ctrl+Shift+End selects everything to the bottom of the document. Try a few of those in your practice file, and press a bare arrow key afterward to collapse the selection away. Selecting text touches nothing until you act on it; marking and unmarking is free.

Now the second way, and if you remember one thing from this chapter make it this one. Put your cursor somewhere, and press F8. QUILL says it is starting a selection. Now move — plain arrows, Ctrl+arrows, End, anything, with no Shift held — and the selection grows from where you pressed F8 to wherever you go. When the selection covers what you meant, just act on it, or press F8 again to switch the mode off. Escape also cancels it. This exists because holding Shift across a three-paragraph journey is genuinely awkward, and a selection you can steer with free hands is calmer to get right.

QUILL also has commands that select a natural piece of text in one stroke, without any steering. Ctrl+Shift+W selects the word under the cursor. Ctrl+Shift+E selects the current line. Ctrl+Shift+H selects the current paragraph. Try the paragraph one: put your cursor anywhere inside a paragraph, press Ctrl+Shift+H, and the whole paragraph is marked.

Two companions round this out. Ctrl+Shift+Y speaks the current selection, so you can confirm exactly what is marked before you act on it — worth its weight the first time you are about to delete something. And Ctrl+Shift+A unselects, leaving your cursor where it is, for when you marked something and changed your mind.

Practice: select a word with Ctrl+Shift+W. Select a paragraph with Ctrl+Shift+H, and press Ctrl+Shift+Y to hear it read back. Then press F8, walk the cursor down two paragraphs with plain arrows, hear the selection grow, and press Escape to let it go.

Keep three: Shift plus any movement for small selections, F8 for big ones, and Ctrl+Shift+Y to hear what you have marked. Next chapter, we finally do something with a selection.

Chapter 6: Cut, copy, paste, and the key that forgives

These four keys are the oldest keys in computing, and QUILL uses the same ones as everything else: Ctrl+C copies the selection, Ctrl+X cuts it — copies it and removes it — and Ctrl+V pastes at the cursor. If you know them already, glance at the second half of this chapter, because that part is QUILL’s own.

If they are newer to you, walk it once with the book. In your practice file, select a sentence — Ctrl+Space selects the sentence under the cursor, or use any method from the last chapter. Press Ctrl+C. Nothing seems to happen, but the sentence is now held on the clipboard. Move to the bottom of the document with Ctrl+End, press Enter for a fresh line, and press Ctrl+V. The sentence appears. That is the entire trick: mark, copy or cut, go somewhere, paste. The clipboard holds one thing at a time, and it is shared with every program on the computer, so a sentence copied in QUILL can be pasted into an email.

Now the forgiving key. Press Ctrl+Z. The paste you just did is undone — the sentence is gone from the bottom. Press Ctrl+Z again and again, and each press takes back one more edit, walking backward through everything you have done. Press Ctrl+Y and it re-does what undo took back. Nothing you type or delete or paste in the editor is beyond Ctrl+Z’s reach.

Understand what this means for how boldly you can work. You do not need to be careful in QUILL. Try the edit; if it is wrong, Ctrl+Z. Move the paragraph; if it reads worse, Ctrl+Z. Every mistake in the editor is a rented mistake. People who trust undo edit better, not because they err less, but because trying things is how good text happens.

QUILL adds one refinement worth knowing today. Sometimes you undo and are not sure what just came back or went away — especially after several undos in a row. Alt+Shift+F3 is Undo and Say What Changed: it undoes one step and tells you out loud what that step was. When you are unwinding a series of edits and counting on your ears, use that instead of bare Ctrl+Z.

And one honest paste for the modern world: text copied from web pages drags its formatting along. Ctrl+Shift+V pastes the words only, stripped clean. When pasting from a browser into your writing, Ctrl+Shift+V is nearly always the one you meant.

Practice the confidence more than the keys: cut a paragraph from one place, paste it somewhere it does not belong, listen to it there, and undo your way back to safety.

Keep four: Ctrl+C, Ctrl+X, Ctrl+V — and above all Ctrl+Z, the reason none of the others are scary.

Chapter 7: Finding and replacing

Somewhere in a long document is the sentence you need to fix, and arrowing through everything to reach it is not a plan. Finding is a skill of its own, and it is the last piece of what I would call the survival set — after this chapter, you can genuinely live in this editor.

Press Ctrl+F. The Find window opens with a box for the text you are hunting. Type a word you know is in your practice file, and press Enter. QUILL jumps to the first place that word appears and reads you the line, so you have some context around the hit. The Find window is still open; press Enter again to go to the next hit, or use the buttons to go forward and back. Press Escape when you are done, and you are back in the editor at the place you found.

Most of the time you do not need the window at all after the first search. F3 repeats the last search from wherever you are — next match, no dialog. Shift+F3 goes to the previous match. This makes checking every mention of a name feel like flipping through index cards: F3, listen, F3, listen.

If the word is not there, QUILL says so plainly. Not found means not found — check the spelling, try a shorter fragment. Searching for a fragment is often smarter than a whole word: hunting “recei” finds both “receive” and “received”, spelled either way.

Now replacing. Press Ctrl+H, and the Replace window opens with two boxes: what to find, and what to put in its place. Here is the one piece of real advice in this chapter: replace one at a time, not all at once, until you have seen a few. Find the next hit, hear it in its sentence, replace it, move on. The Replace All button does the entire document in one stroke, and it is exactly right when you have renamed a project and forty instances need the same change — but words live inside other words, and replacing “cat” with “dog” everywhere also turns “catalog” into “dogalog”. Ctrl+Z does take back a replace-all, so even that mistake is rented. But taste a few before you buy them all.

Practice: search for a word with Ctrl+F, walk three hits with F3, then use Ctrl+H to change one word to another a couple of times, hearing each one before you say yes.

Keep three: Ctrl+F to find, F3 for next, Ctrl+H to replace. That completes the survival set — everything from here on is comfort, speed, and reach.

Chapter 8: Spelling

You could write forever without this chapter; misspelled words save to disk just fine. But a spell check before anyone else reads your work is cheap insurance, and QUILL’s is built for checking by ear.

Open your practice file and plant a mistake on purpose — type “freind” somewhere. Now press F7. The spell check dialog opens on the first word QUILL does not recognize, reads it, usually reads the sentence around it, and offers suggestions. Arrow through the suggestions until you hear “friend,” and accept it. The dialog moves to the next problem word on its own. When there is nothing left, it says so, and you are done. Escape leaves the dialog at any point.

The choices in the dialog are few and honest. Change fixes this occurrence. Ignore skips this one without fixing it. And Add sends the word to your personal dictionary, which is the choice people underuse: your own name, your town, the odd product name you type weekly — the first time the checker trips on one, add it, and it is never questioned again. Your dictionary belongs to you, and a word added is a tiny permanent improvement to every future check.

There is also a way to handle spelling without the ceremony of a dialog. Ctrl+F7 jumps the cursor to the next questionable word right in the editor; fix it by hand, or press Ctrl+F7 again to keep touring. Ctrl+Shift+F7 goes to the previous one. And when the cursor is already sitting on a word you know is fine, Ctrl+Alt+F9 adds it to your dictionary on the spot, no dialog at all. That trio suits the way real proofreading happens: skimming your own text, pouncing where something is off.

One neighbor worth introducing while we are here: with the cursor on a word, Shift+F7 opens a thesaurus and offers alternatives. When a sentence has said “important” three times, this is the key that rescues it.

Practice: plant two misspellings, run F7 and fix them both, then add some word the dictionary does not know — your surname is a good candidate — with Ctrl+Alt+F9.

Keep two habits: F7 for a full pass before your text meets its readers, and Add whenever the checker questions a word that is actually right.

Chapter 9: A pause, and what comes next

No new keys in this chapter. It is here because you have just crossed a real line, and the book should say so rather than rushing past it.

Count what your hands now know. You can make documents, save them, and get them back. You can cross a long document, mark exactly the text you mean, and move it around. You can undo anything, find anything, replace carefully, and run a spell check by ear. When you are lost, F1 explains where you are, and Ctrl+Shift+P finds any command from a half-remembered word.

That is not “the basics.” That is the actual job. A large share of everything ever written was written with exactly the set of skills you have right now, and if you closed this book today, QUILL would serve you well for years. Nothing in the remaining chapters is required. It is all leverage.

Here is what remains, so you can choose your own order. Chapter ten gives documents a skeleton — headings — and then lets you travel by that skeleton, which changes what long documents feel like. Chapter eleven is bookmarks: leaving markers in your text and snapping back to them. Chapter twelve has QUILL read your writing aloud to you, which is the single best editing trick this book knows. Chapter thirteen is working in several documents at once. Chapter fourteen is the honest chapter about crashes and safety nets. Chapter fifteen makes QUILL fit you — keys, chattiness, preferences. Chapter sixteen introduces the one unusual key I promised in the introduction. And chapter seventeen tells you where to go when this book runs out.

They are written in a sensible order, but they do not lean on each other much. If reading your work aloud is what made you install this program, jump to chapter twelve; nothing will feel missing.

Take the break. The next chapter is here whenever you are.

Chapter 10: Headings, and traveling by structure

A document with no headings is one long corridor: to know what is where, you walk it. Headings turn the corridor into rooms with names, and once your documents have rooms, QUILL can carry you between them in single keystrokes. This chapter builds the rooms first, then does the traveling.

A heading in QUILL carries a level from one to six. Level one is the top — usually the title, one per document. Level twos are the major sections. Threes live inside twos. Most working documents never need more than three levels, and plenty do fine with just twos.

Build one now. Make a new document with Ctrl+N. Type “My report” on the first line, and with the cursor still on that line, press Ctrl+Alt+1. That line is now a heading, level one. Press Enter, type “Background”, and press Ctrl+Alt+2. Press Enter and type an ordinary sentence or two — body text needs no key at all. Then add two more level-two sections the same way: “Findings” with a sentence under it, and “Conclusion” with another. Ctrl+Alt+3 through Ctrl+Alt+6 make the deeper levels when you someday want them, and if you overshoot — a heading that should have been plain text — Ctrl+Alt+0 turns the line back into body text.

Now the payoff. Press Ctrl+Home to go to the top, then press Ctrl+Alt+H. That is Next Heading: the cursor jumps to “Background”, skipping the body text entirely. Press it again — “Findings”. Again — “Conclusion”. Ctrl+Alt+Shift+H walks backward the same way. Four keystrokes just toured a document that could have been forty pages, and it is the same four keystrokes whether it is one page or four hundred.

One more view of the same idea. Press Ctrl+Shift+O, and the Outline Navigator opens: your headings as a list, nothing else. Arrow through it, pick a heading, press Enter, and you land there in the document. When a report gets genuinely large, this list is how you hold its shape in mind — the table of contents that maintains itself.

The habit that makes all this pay is small: when you start anything longer than a page, give its sections headings as you go. Not for looks — headings are how you and QUILL will both navigate it next week.

Keep three: Ctrl+Alt+2 to make a section heading, Ctrl+Alt+H to travel by headings, and Ctrl+Shift+O when you want the whole map at once.

Chapter 11: Bookmarks — leaving a trail

Chapter four gave you Alt+Left, the key that returns you to where you just were. Bookmarks are the deliberate version of the same comfort: instead of QUILL remembering your trail automatically, you plant a marker on purpose, at a place you know you will need again.

The simplest one is the temporary bookmark, and it covers most real needs. Put your cursor anywhere in a document and press Ctrl+Alt+J. QUILL confirms the spot is marked. Now wander — Ctrl+End, arrow around, edit something far away. When you want your spot back, press Ctrl+Shift+J, and the cursor returns exactly there. One marker, two keys, no bookkeeping. The classic moment for it: you are mid-sentence and suddenly need to check a paragraph near the top. Drop the marker, go look, snap back, finish the sentence.

When one marker is not enough — a long document where you keep returning to several places — QUILL has numbered bookmarks. Press Ctrl+Shift+B on a line to set one there; do it somewhere else to set the next. F2 hops the cursor forward to the next bookmark in the document, and Shift+F2 to the previous one, so a handful of numbered marks become stepping stones you can walk in both directions. And when you have marked more spots than your memory is carrying, Alt+Shift+G opens a list of all your bookmarks; pick one and press Enter to land on it.

Two honest notes so the feature never surprises you. Numbered bookmarks are saved with QUILL and survive closing the file — set marks in a novel manuscript today and they greet you tomorrow. And the temporary bookmark is exactly what its name says: one slot, overwritten each time you press Ctrl+Alt+J, meant for right now rather than posterity.

Practice in your headed report from last chapter: drop the temporary mark in “Findings”, jump to the top, come back with Ctrl+Shift+J. Then set numbered bookmarks on two different sections and walk between them with F2 and Shift+F2.

Keep the pair: Ctrl+Alt+J to mark, Ctrl+Shift+J to snap back. Reach for the numbered ones the day a document is big enough to need a trail rather than a spot.

Chapter 12: Hearing your writing

Here is the best editing advice this book contains, and it happens to need a computer: listen to your own writing being read back, at reading speed, without you doing the reading. Your eyes — and your inner voice — smooth over what is actually on the page. You wrote it, so you read what you meant. A voice that is not you reads what is there. Doubled words, a sentence that never ends, the word “that” four times in two lines: things you would miss forever on the page are unmissable in the air.

If you use a screen reader, you might reasonably ask why QUILL needs a reading voice of its own. The difference is the job. Your screen reader follows your focus and tells you where you are; QUILL’s Read Aloud is a performance of the document, flowing on without your hands on the keys, while you lean back and just be the audience. Different tool, different posture — and the posture is the point. Editing ears work best when the hands are still.

The keys in this chapter use the QUILL key, which chapter sixteen explains properly. The short version, enough for today: press Ctrl+Shift+Grave — the grave is the back-tick key just above Tab, and you press this all together like any other shortcut, then release it. QUILL plays a soft double-tone, meaning “I’m listening for one more key.” Then press the second key on its own. That whole two-step gesture is written “QUILL Key + R” in QUILL’s menus, and spoken that way here.

So: open a document with a few paragraphs — your practice file or the report from chapter ten. Press the QUILL key, then R. Read Aloud begins from your cursor and flows onward. Let it run a little. The same gesture, QUILL Key + R again, pauses it, and once more resumes. When you have heard enough, QUILL Key + Shift+R stops it entirely.

Two smaller companions do the same job at different sizes. Alt+F8 is Read All — the whole document from the top, regardless of where your cursor is, which is the natural way to take in a finished draft. And Ctrl+Shift+Y, which you met in the selection chapter, speaks just the current selection — right for testing whether one rewritten sentence finally sounds like a sentence.

The practice for this chapter is really a habit for life: before anything important leaves your hands — the email that matters, the cover letter, the chapter — have QUILL read it to you once, start to finish, and fix what your ears catch. Ears catch what eyes forgive.

Keep one gesture and one habit: QUILL Key + R to start and pause the reading, and a full listen before anything important ships.

Chapter 13: More than one document

Real work rarely lives in one file. You are writing in one document and checking notes in another, or copying lines from an old draft into a new one. QUILL keeps every open document in the same window, and this chapter is about moving between them without losing your place in any of them.

Have your practice file open, and open the report from chapter ten as well — Ctrl+O, or File, then Open Recent. Two documents are now open, and the window title tells you which one you are looking at.

The main key is Ctrl+Tab: it switches to your next open document. With two documents, it simply flips between them — press it a few times and hear the title alternate. With more open, Ctrl+Tab walks the whole ring, and Ctrl+Shift+Tab walks it the other way. Each document keeps its own cursor position while you are away; flipping to notes and back does not cost you your sentence.

When several documents are open, the ring gets slow, and QUILL has a faster door: each open document has a number, and Alt+1 jumps straight to document one, Alt+2 to document two, and so on up through Alt+9. The Window menu lists your open documents with their numbers, so you never have to guess — and after a day of this, Alt+1 for “the main thing I am writing” and Alt+2 for “the notes” becomes muscle rather than thought.

Try the flow that makes this real: in your report, put the cursor in the Findings section. Flip to the practice file with Ctrl+Tab, copy a sentence with Ctrl+C, flip back, and paste it in. That round trip — flip, take, flip back, drop — is nine tenths of everything people do with two documents.

Closing is the same key you already know: Ctrl+W closes the document you are in, asking about unsaved changes first, and leaves the rest open. After a long session with many files open, Ctrl+Shift+F4 closes every document except the one you are standing in — and if any of the others have unsaved changes, QUILL asks once about the lot, offering to save all with one answer rather than interrogating you file by file.

Keep two: Ctrl+Tab to flip between documents, Alt+1 through Alt+9 to jump by number. Your notes can stay open all day without ever being in the way.

Chapter 14: When something goes wrong

This chapter is about crashes, power cuts, and mistakes discovered too late. Nobody plans for these, so the only honest time to learn the safety nets is now, while nothing is wrong.

Start with what QUILL does on its own. As you work on a document with unsaved changes, QUILL keeps recovery snapshots of it in the background, without being asked. If QUILL is ever cut down mid-sentence — the machine loses power, Windows restarts itself overnight, the program crashes — then the next time you start QUILL, it offers you a choice: here is what was open when things ended badly, would you like it back? Take it, and your almost-lost words return. Nothing needed from you in advance. It is worth knowing this before you ever see it, because the offer appearing after a bad evening is a moment people meet at their most rattled — and the right answer is usually simply yes.

To be clear about the division of labor: Ctrl+S is still the plan. The recovery offer is the net under the trapeze, and nets are for falling, not for living on. Save when you pause; let recovery be the thing you almost never need.

The second net catches a different kind of loss: the file that was saved, but saved wrong. You deleted a section on Tuesday, saved, and on Thursday realize you needed it — Ctrl+Z cannot help, because undo history belongs to the editing session, and that session is long over. For this, QUILL keeps earlier versions of your files. Press Ctrl+Alt+Shift+E, Restore Previous Version, and QUILL shows the versions it holds for the current document, labeled by when they were saved. You can bring one back — and Tuesday’s section with it.

The third net is the smallest and the one you will use most. QUILL speaks — confirmations, warnings, results — and speech vanishes the moment it ends. When something was said and you missed it, or you half-heard a warning while typing, press Alt+Shift+E. That is the Spoken Echo: a list of the last things QUILL announced, newest first, that you can arrow through at your own pace and even copy from. Missed announcements stop being missed; they are just in the Echo, waiting.

Nothing to practice here, and I would not wish the practice on you. Just carry the three facts: after a crash, QUILL offers your work back — say yes. For a bad save discovered days later, Ctrl+Alt+Shift+E reaches earlier versions. And when speech got away from you, Alt+Shift+E replays it.

Chapter 15: Making QUILL yours

Everything so far used QUILL exactly as it installs. That default is a fine place to live, so this chapter is not homework — it is a map of the three adjustments that matter most, for whenever a default starts to chafe.

The front door is Preferences, on Ctrl+Comma. It is a window of settings organized into pages: how files open, how spell check behaves, what QUILL says and when, and a great deal more. You do not browse a window like that; you arrive with a question. And you already own the tool for questions — F1. Land on any setting, press F1, and it explains what the setting does and what changing it would mean. Preferences plus F1 is how you tune a program without reading its manual. Escape backs you out, and nothing changes unless you changed it.

The second adjustment is the keyboard itself. Every shortcut this book has taught is a default, not a law. Ctrl+Alt+Shift+R opens the Keymap Editor, where you can search for any command and give it the key you wish it had. Two details make it trustworthy. You can choose Record Keys and simply press the combination you want, rather than spelling it out. And if the key you press already belongs to another command, QUILL tells you which one, by name, and offers to move the key properly — nothing is ever silently overwritten. If some gesture from an editor you used for years is wired into your hands, spend the one minute making QUILL match your hands. You will save that minute back within the week.

The third adjustment is how much QUILL talks. Some people want a running narration of everything; others want silence broken only by problems. Open the Command Palette with Ctrl+Shift+P, type “verbosity”, and you will find the settings that govern how chatty QUILL is, ready to be tuned in either direction. There are also sound events — QUILL can mark moments like a save or a search miss with a short tone instead of words, or alongside them, and Alt+Shift+M switches sound notifications on and off as a whole. Whether a day goes better with tones, words, both, or neither is entirely a matter of taste, and it is your taste that gets to decide.

If you adjust nothing today, that is a fine outcome. The point of the chapter is smaller: when a default does bother you, it is not a fact of life. It is a setting, F1 will explain it, and five minutes will fix it.

Keep one key and one idea: Ctrl+Comma opens Preferences, and F1 inside it means you never have to guess.

Chapter 16: The QUILL key

You met this key briefly in chapter twelve, where it started Read Aloud. Now, properly: the QUILL key is the one genuinely unusual thing on QUILL’s keyboard, it unlocks the program’s larger features, and it works differently from every other shortcut you know.

An ordinary shortcut is one gesture: hold modifiers, press a letter, done. The QUILL key is instead a prefix — a way of getting QUILL’s full attention first. Press Ctrl+Shift+Grave (that back-tick key above Tab, all pressed together like any chord, then released). QUILL answers with its soft double-tone: “listening.” Now press one more key, alone, and that second key picks the command. Menus write this two-step as “QUILL Key + R”, “QUILL Key

  • G“, and so on. Why would a program complicate a keystroke this way? Arithmetic. The ordinary combinations — Ctrl plus this, Ctrl and Shift plus that — are nearly all spoken for, in QUILL and in Windows itself. The prefix opens a whole second keyboard: every letter, fresh again, and QUILL uses that space for its bigger machinery. You already know QUILL Key + R, reading aloud. QUILL Key + D starts dictation — speaking your words instead of typing them, on machines set up for it. QUILL Key + I asks QUILL to describe an image. QUILL Key + Y turns a whole document into spoken audio you can keep. None of these need to be learned today; what should settle in is the shape — prefix, tone, one letter — because every big feature you meet from now on will speak it.

Two useful corners of the mechanism. If you press the QUILL key and change your mind, Escape cancels the prefix, and pressing it by accident costs nothing — the little tone, then Escape, and no harm done. And you never have to memorize what the second keys are: press the QUILL key and then the question mark, and a cheat sheet opens listing every chord the prefix knows. QUILL Key + ? is the directory for the whole neighborhood.

Try the shape three times, none of them dangerous. QUILL Key + R to start your document reading, and again to pause it. QUILL Key + ? to open the cheat sheet and arrow down what lives here — just looking. And once, press the QUILL key and then Escape, so your hands know that backing out is free.

Keep the shape, not a list: Ctrl+Shift+Grave, the tone, one letter. And QUILL Key + ? whenever you wonder what else it can say.

Chapter 17: Where to go from here

This book ends here, but it was never the whole story — it is the floor of the house. You can stand on it. Here is what is above, and honestly what each thing is good for.

The follow-along tutorials, on QUILL’s website under Tutorials, are the natural next room. Where this book taught the editor, each tutorial walks one real project end to end at the keyboard: rescuing a scanned PDF into clean text, turning a document into an audiobook, keeping a linked vault of notes, listening to internet radio and podcasts without leaving your editor. When one of those is a thing you actually want, an hour with its tutorial gets you there.

The QUILL Cast is the same teaching in audio form — an episode series you can subscribe to in any podcast app, with a full transcript for every episode. Episodes are short; a commute fits two of them. It suits the moments when your hands are busy but your ears are free.

The full user guide is the reference book, open from inside QUILL with Ctrl+Shift+F1. Nobody reads it cover to cover, and nobody should. It is where the complete answer lives when you need everything QUILL knows about one topic. Ask it questions; do not move into it.

And QUILL can do things this book deliberately left alone: take dictation, describe images, translate, sit an AI assistant beside your work for the days you want one — all of it switched off until you ask. When you get curious, the Help menu’s tutorials, on Ctrl+Alt+F1, include gentle introductions, and the setup wizards walk you through anything that needs installing. Curiosity is the only prerequisite.

If you ever need a person rather than a document, Ctrl+Alt+F2 — Get Help from Support — opens a short form and hands it to your own mail program, addressed to people who read what arrives. Real problems and honest suggestions are both welcome there; a report like the one that caused this book to be written is how the program gets better.

Last thing, and then the book will stop talking. Six weeks from now, open the Command Palette and just arrow through it for two minutes. You will find a command you did not know you had, and by then you will simply take it and use it — because somewhere along these seventeen chapters, this stopped being software you were learning and became a tool you own. That was the whole idea.

Thanks for listening. Go write something.

Quillin Snippet Wizard

QUILL Quillin Wizard

Quillin Snippet Wizard

Build a snippet-only (Layer 1) Quillin without writing a single line of code. Fill in the form, then copy or download your manifest.json.

A snippet Quillin adds menu items and keyboard shortcuts that insert text - with optional placeholders like \${selection}, \${date}, \${word_at_cursor}, and \${uuid} - into your document. No Python required. Follow the tutorial to go further with Python handlers.

Responsible AI Use

Responsible AI Use

Responsible and Ethical AI Use

QUILL includes optional AI-assisted features. These features are designed to be user-controlled and review-first.

Responsible-use policy
  • AI output is advisory, not authoritative.
  • You must review all generated output before applying, publishing, or sharing it.
  • You are fully responsible for downstream use of AI-generated content.
  • Do not use AI features to violate privacy, law, policy, or intellectual-property rights.
  • Avoid sending sensitive, regulated, or confidential data to cloud providers unless you are explicitly authorized.
Trust controls in QUILL
  • explicit user-initiated AI actions
  • approval flow before document-changing actions
  • plain-language connection and status messaging
  • startup trust and consent acknowledgement
  • secure key handling via Windows Credential Manager (with encrypted fallback)
Provider boundaries

When a cloud provider is selected, prompts you send are processed under that provider’s terms and retention policy. QUILL cannot override provider-side policy behavior.

For highest privacy, prefer local model backends when available.

Security Policy

Security Policy

Security Policy

Supported versions

Security fixes are prioritized on the latest release line in main.

Version line

Security support

Current release (main)

Supported

Older releases

Best effort only

Reporting a vulnerability

Please report suspected vulnerabilities privately. Do not open a public issue for security problems.

  • Email: support@communityaccess.org
  • Subject: QUILL security report If your report includes sensitive details, note that in the subject/body and we will coordinate a safer exchange path.

Include the following details:

  • A description of the issue and impact.
  • Reproduction steps or proof of concept.
  • Affected version/commit.
  • Any suggested mitigation.
  • Whether you believe this is remotely exploitable or local-only.
Response expectations

Target response windows:

  • Acknowledgement: within 3 business days.
  • Initial triage: within 7 business days.
  • Follow-up cadence: at least weekly until resolution or mitigation.
  • Coordinated disclosure: agreed after fix readiness. Please do not disclose the issue publicly until maintainers confirm a fix and disclosure plan.
Scope guidance

Security reports are most useful when they involve:

  • Unauthorized access to protected data

  • Privilege escalation

  • Remote code execution paths

  • Unsafe network or update trust behavior

  • Secret exposure in logs, diagnostics, or crash artifacts Out-of-scope examples (generally):

  • Purely theoretical findings without a plausible exploit path

  • Reports that require unrealistic local setup not used by QUILL users

  • Best-practice suggestions without a concrete vulnerability

Safe harbor for good-faith research

We support good-faith security research intended to improve user safety. Please:

  • Avoid privacy violations, destructive testing, or service disruption.
  • Test only what is necessary to demonstrate the issue.
  • Keep findings private until coordinated disclosure is agreed. If you follow these expectations in good faith, we will treat your research as authorized for this policy’s purposes.
Security expectations for contributors

All contributors should follow these baseline practices:

  • Never commit secrets, tokens, credentials, or private keys.

  • Avoid logging document content or sensitive user data.

  • Keep networked behavior explicit and user-initiated.

  • Validate external input and fail safely.

  • Use dependency updates intentionally and review changelogs for risk.

  • Keep cloud endpoints on HTTPS; allow HTTP only for local-only runtimes.

  • Ensure diagnostics and logs redact API keys, bearer tokens, and equivalent secrets. Related project docs:

  • CONTRIBUTING.md

  • CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md

  • PRIVACY.md

  • RESPONSIBLE_AI_USE.md

Secret handling baseline

QUILL stores AI API keys in Windows Credential Manager when available. If Credential Manager is unavailable, QUILL falls back to DPAPI-encrypted local storage. Plaintext API key storage is not permitted.

Security automation baseline
  • .github/workflows/security-ci.yml runs dependency audit, secret scanning, and SBOM generation.
  • .github/workflows/windows-release.yml publishes release metadata plus SBOM artifacts.

QUILL accessible software, built with you

No account, and no sign-in — not here and not anywhere else. Fill in the form on this page, press Send suggestion, and it reaches us directly.

What happens next
